extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IP litigators, judges, policymakers, and legal scholars interested in the America Invents Act and patent litigation practice
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and applying the America Invents Act amendments to Title 35 (patent statutes), including how specific sections (best mode, marking, false marking, advice of counsel, joinder, claim-scope statements, reexamination) affect litigation, remedies, and USPTO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-mode discovery / evidentiary inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery on 'best mode' involves examining every document the inventor wrote—or read—relating to a mode for carrying out the invention; it is a confluence of 'what did the inventor know and when did the inventor know it' with 'what might, therefore, the inventor contemplated and when might those contemplations have taken place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage cautions that best-mode discovery can require intrusive fact-finding into the inventor's knowledge and mental state across time. The legislative debate reflects concerns that best-mode discovery produces burdensome inquiry into inventor documents and communications. (Cites testimony and hearings expressing both support for and criticism of the best-mode requirement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA §15: elimination of best-mode as basis for invalidity/enforceability in proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15(c) of the AIA makes the section’s best-mode changes applicable to all 'proceedings' commenced after enactment of the Act and removes failure to disclose best mode under §112 as a basis for canceling or holding invalid or unenforceable a patent claim in litigation and post-grant proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'proceedings' was chosen to make changes applicable immediately in litigation and post-grant reviews. Legislative history shows Congress removed best mode as a litigation basis but did not explain why it did not simply repeal the requirement entirely from all contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of AIA on §119(a) and foreign priority / 'symmetry' rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts had interpreted 35 U.S.C. §119(a) to require a foreign application to disclose the best mode to obtain U.S. priority, AIA §15 does not expressly repeal best mode from §119(a); however, because §120's best-mode language was repealed, the symmetry rationale requires reading best mode out of §119(a) as well, and §119(a)'s text ('shall have the same effect') supports that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should understand that post-AIA, a foreign priority application that fails to disclose the best mode should still be entitled to U.S. priority when the corresponding domestic parent would be—because §120 no longer makes best-mode disclosure a prerequisite. This is a textual and symmetry-based interpretive consequence discussed in the legislative history.

rubrics_metrics.name: §287: Marking requirement limits on damages (including virtual marking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 287(a) limits recoverable damages for a patented product to those damages incurred after the infringer received actual notice, unless the product was marked as patented; the AIA (sec. 16(a)) allows the patent number in marking to be replaced with 'an address of a posting on the Internet ... that associates the patented article with the number of the patent' (virtual marking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA, 'patent' or 'pat.' and patent number had to be affixed to product or packaging. Virtual marking permits a URL linking the product to patent numbers, saving costs for retroactive patenting and facilitating marking for small products. The burden remains on the patent holder to demonstrate that marking was effective. Note also §287 does not apply to process/method patents or to a patent owner who neither sells nor authorizes sales of articles covered by the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: §292: Repeal of false-marking qui tam and limits on enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA repealed the false-marking qui tam action (sec. 16(b)), retained a civil penalty but limited enforcement so 'Only the United States may sue for [this] penalty,' and provides that marking a product with an expired patent that once applied to the product 'is not a violation.' The changes are retroactive to all cases pending or commenced on/after enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress replaced private qui tam suits (which had produced mass nuisance litigation, often over expired patents or minor marking) with enforcement limited to injured parties seeking compensatory damages and the United States for the statutory fine. The legislative history explains this change responds to a surge of abusive qui tam filings (e.g., many suits based on expired patents) and seeks to curb opportunistic litigation seeking per-article statutory fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of remedies for false marking post-AIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-AIA, parties that have suffered a competitive injury as a result of false marking may seek compensatory damages; the United States may pursue the statutory per-article fine. Private qui tam suits by unrelated third parties were eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intent is to limit litigation to parties with actual competitive harm and to prevent fee-seeking qui tam suits by unrelated private actors. Legislative commentary emphasizes avoiding disproportionate litigation incentives that do not reflect real harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: §298: Advice-of-counsel evidence barred for willfulness/inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: New 35 U.S.C. §298 provides that the failure of an infringer to obtain advice of counsel, or to present such advice to the court or jury, may not be used to prove willful infringement or intent to induce infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 298 protects attorney-client privilege and reduces pressure to obtain litigation-driven counsel opinions. It applies to findings of both willfulness and inducement and legislatively abrogates Broadcom v. Qualcomm. Practical caveat: because §298 was enacted without its own effective date, its applicability depends on the AIA's default effective-date rule (it applies to patents issued on or after the default effective date), which can create timing issues in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: §299: Limits on joinder of accused infringers and consolidation of trials
rubrics_metrics.description: New 35 U.S.C. §299 restricts joinder and consolidation: accused infringers may be joined or consolidated only if (1) any right to relief is asserted against the parties jointly, severally, or in the alternative with respect to or arising out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences relating to the same accused product or process; and (2) questions of fact common to all defendants will arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder may not be based solely on allegations that each defendant infringed the same patent(s). The provision also permits a defendant to waive these limitations. §299 was intended to curb mass multi-defendant suits (often used by non-practicing entities) and to limit consolidation under Rule 42 as well as joinder under Rule 20, legislatively abrogating the minority Rule 20 interpretation that had allowed joining many unrelated defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: §301(a)(2) & (c)-(d): Submission and use of patent-owner claim-scope statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA allows any party to submit to the USPTO 'statements of the patent owner filed in a proceeding before a Federal court or the Office in which the patent owner took a position on the scope of any claim of a particular patent.' Submitters must include related documents, pleadings, or evidence from the proceeding that address the written statement. These materials 'shall not be considered by the Office for any purpose other than to determine the proper meaning of a patent claim' in reexamination, inter partes, or post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansion helps the Office identify inconsistent claim constructions by patent owners across forums (e.g., district court vs. PTAB). The Committee emphasized these statements are not intended as a basis for initiating reexamination proceedings; reexaminations remain institutionable only on the basis of 'patents or printed publications.' The legislative history notes the scope of 'patent or printed publication' prior art for reexamination remains coextensive with section 102 prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: §303: Director-initiated ex parte reexamination standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Amended §303 allows the Director to institute an ex parte reexamination on the Director's own initiative if a substantial new question of patentability is raised by patents or publications (and expands the sources the Director may use to include citations authorized by §302).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously the Director was limited to patents/printed publications the Director discovered or that were cited under §301; the AIA broadened the Director's ability to identify substantial new questions of patentability and to order reexamination sua sponte. The Committee framed this as an expansion of the ex parte reexamination procedure to allow more proactive Office action when patents/printed publications show new questions of patentability.
